title: Act IV, Scene VII

teacherSummary.text: Claudius explains to Laertes why he did not punish Hamlet publicly. News arrives that Hamlet has returned. They plot a fencing match with an unbated, poisoned sword and a poisoned cup. Gertrude reports Ophelia drowned.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act IV, Scene VII,” how does Shakespeare show the plot against Hamlet? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act IV, Scene VII, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of the plot against Hamlet? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the plot in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act IV, Scene VII develops the idea of the plot against Hamlet. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of plot and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act IV, Scene VII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its plot shape the reader's understanding of the plot against Hamlet. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act IV, Scene VII suggests about the plot against Hamlet. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's plot and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses plot in Act IV, Scene VII to complicate the reader's understanding of the plot against Hamlet. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act IV, Scene VII within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of the plot against Hamlet responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act IV, Scene VII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of the plot against Hamlet follows or bends those conventions, using the plot as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act IV, Scene VII and its treatment of the plot against Hamlet. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's plot and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act IV, Scene VII as evidence for a larger claim about the plot against Hamlet in Hamlet. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act IV, Scene VII as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of the plot against Hamlet. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Hamlet.

satQuestions.passage:
O, for two special reasons;
Which may to you, perhaps, seem much unsinew’d,
But yet to me they are strong. The queen his mother
Lives almost by his looks; and for myself—
My virtue or my plague, be it either which—
She’s so conjunctive to my life and soul,
That, as the star moves not but in his sphere,
I could not but by her. The other motive,
Why to a public count I might not go,
Is the great love the general gender bear him;
Who, dipping all his faults in their affection,
Would, like the spring that turneth wood to stone,
Convert his gyves to graces; so that my arrows,
Too slightly timber’d for so loud a wind,
Would have reverted to my bow again,
And not where I had aim’d them.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: disease and rot
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Denmark is sick: "Something is rotten in the state of Denmark"; corruption spreads like poison and ulcers. In this scene: “my lord. But let him come; / It warms the very sickness in my heart, / That I shall live and tell him to” (Act IV, Scene VII, Laertes (speech 12)).

segments.script: Annotate the scene for plot, characterization (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this scene suggest about the plot against Hamlet? Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of plot and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: Laertes's readiness for revenge, unlike Hamlet's, has no moral limits. When the text says “There is a willow grows aslant a brook” (Act IV, Scene VII, Queen (speech 36)), it shows this directly. items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: Laertes's readiness for revenge, unlike Hamlet's, has no moral limits. Useful evidence: “To cut his throat i’ the church” (Act IV, Scene VII, Laertes (speech 30)): Laertes's answer when asked what he would do to Hamlet. On imagery: Gertrude's report of Ophelia's drowning: willow, flowers, her clothes "spread wide," singing as she sinks. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Gertrude reports Ophelia's drowning; whether it was suicide is debated later. Use the safe-messaging script.
contentNotes.studentPreview: This scene reports a young woman's death by drowning. Support is available if this is hard to read.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “Why does Gertrude describe the death so gently?”

safeMessaging.teacherScript: Discuss the character's despair and what the text does with it; do not dwell on methods. Before the lesson, remind students that support is available and how to reach the counselor. Check in privately with any student who seems affected and follow your school's referral protocol.
safeMessaging.studentResource: If you or someone you know is struggling or thinking about suicide, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, U.S.) or talk with a school counselor today.
safeMessaging.counselorPrompt: Let a counselor know in advance that this scene is being taught.
